    • VARIABLE_EXPANSION

    • PARAMETER_FORMATTING

      public static final Config.DisableableFeature PARAMETER_FORMATTING
      Disables parameter formatting, i.e. the Formatter substitution of a method's arguments into its value — %s and %d, as String.format(java.lang.String, java.lang.Object...) does.

      Not MessageFormat's {0}, which this javadoc claimed until 2.0.0 and which the library has never supported; asking for it is #118, still open.

    • RELAXED_BINDING

      public static final Config.DisableableFeature RELAXED_BINDING
      Disables the relaxed binding, so that the annotated method — or every method of the annotated interface — reads the key it resolves to and no other spelling of it.

      On by default: the four forms a key may be written in are a closed set, tried only after the key itself, and a configuration whose file already agrees with its interface never reaches them. Switch it off where a file deliberately holds two spellings of one name as two different properties, or where the extra lookups on a property that is absent are worth removing.

      Three of the four keep the shape of the key — kebab, snake, camel — and the fourth is the name the setting has as an environment variable, where a dot cannot appear: every character that is not a letter or a digit becomes an underscore, so server.maxThreads is looked for as SERVER_MAX_THREADS. One rule, applied in every source rather than only in system:env, which is what makes it possible to say where a value will come from without running the program.

      Since:
      2.0.0

    • VALIDATION

      public static final Config.DisableableFeature VALIDATION
      Disables the checking of the Bean Validation constraints - @Min, @NotNull and the rest - written on the annotated method, or on every method of the annotated interface.

      It disables the report as well as the check, and that is the point of it: a constraint that nothing checks is otherwise said out loud when the configuration is created, because an annotation that reads like a guarantee and is not one is the failure this library was asked to stop. This annotation is how a configuration says that its constraints are there for somebody else - a framework that reads the same interface, a code generator - and that OWNER is right to leave them alone.

      Since:
      2.0.0

    • isDisabledFor

      public boolean isDisabledFor(Method method)
      Tells whether this feature is disabled for the given method, considering the Config.DisableFeature annotation on the method itself and on the interface declaring it.

      The lookup stops at the interface that declares the method, and deliberately: an interface governs the methods it declares, which is the same rule Config.Prefix follows and the reason a sub-interface cannot change the meaning of the keys its parent declared. Were it to climb, a blanket @DisableFeature(PREFIX) on some base interface would cancel a @Prefix written explicitly two levels below it, which is a negative overruling a positive at a distance. For the question about the configuration object - has this configuration asked for the feature to be off? - see isDisabledFor(Class).

      This method replaces org.aeonbits.owner.util.Util.isFeatureDisabled(Method, DisableableFeature), removed in 2.0.0: the knowledge of Config.DisableFeature now sits next to the annotation it reads.

      Parameters:
      method - the method to inspect.
      Returns:
      true if this feature is disabled for the given method, false otherwise.
      Since:
      2.0.0

    • isDisabledFor

      public boolean isDisabledFor(Class<?> clazz)
      Tells whether this feature is disabled for a configuration object as a whole: the annotation is looked for on the given interface and on every interface above it, nearest first.

      The methods of Accessible are asked this question rather than isDisabledFor(Method): they are declared on Accessible and not on the configuration interface, so the annotation that concerns them is never on their declaring class. A @DisableFeature(VARIABLE_EXPANSION) written on a configuration interface has to reach getProperty and fill as well, and this is how.

      It reads the whole hierarchy since 2.0.0. Before that it read the given interface and nothing above it, so one configuration answered the same question two ways: the annotation written on a super-interface switched the feature off for the methods that interface declares - through isDisabledFor(Method), which finds it on the declaring class - and left it on for getProperty and fill, which ask here. The same property came back expanded or unexpanded depending on which of the two you called.

      Every declaration found is read, not only the nearest one, because this annotation carries a set of features and two interfaces of the same hierarchy may switch off one each: taking the nearest would answer false about a feature a base interface had disabled, only because some interface below it disabled a different one.

      Parameters:
      clazz - the interface to inspect.
      Returns:
      true if this feature is disabled for the given interface, false otherwise.
      Since:
      2.0.0
